analysis.one_liner: Creates government health insurance for every pregnant woman and child under 7, paid for by higher income taxes.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: introduced in February 1992 with two cosponsors, it sat in two House committees and died when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created a new federal health insurance program, run by a new National Children's Health Care Administration, covering every pregnant woman and every child under 7 who is a citizen or lawful resident. It would have covered checkups, immunizations, dental care, hospital and delivery care, prescription drugs, and mental health and therapy services, with no deductibles or copays and no charges above the government payment rate. The program would have been paid for by raising individual income tax rates across the board and raising the corporate rate from 34% to 37%.
analysis.who_benefits: All pregnant women and children under 7, regardless of income. They would get comprehensive coverage — prenatal and delivery care, preventive and dental care, hospital care, prescriptions, mental health and developmental services — with no deductibles, coinsurance, or other cost-sharing, and providers could not bill them above the government rate. The bill also promised providers payment rates fully adequate to keep them from losing income, designed to keep doctors and hospitals participating.

how_it_helps.text: The bill entitled every eligible pregnant woman and child under 7 to health benefits, with enrollment through local health departments and cards issued at birth or during pregnancy.

Coverage included preventive care (checkups, immunizations, dental cleanings and sealants), major medical (hospital care, delivery, physician services, prescription drugs, eyeglasses and hearing aids), and extended services such as mental health, substance abuse, developmental disability treatment, and speech, occupational, and physical therapy.

The program imposed no deductibles, coinsurance, or cost-sharing, and providers were barred from charging patients more than the government payment rate, with exclusion or civil penalties for violators.

Each state would run a community-based outreach system with care coordinators — home visits, help finding a doctor, transportation and appointment help — reimbursed by the federal government, aimed at the finding that about 35% of pregnant women got minimal or no prenatal care.

The bill's findings cited Medicaid's limits: only half of Medicaid-eligible children actually received services, and many children above the poverty line had no employer coverage at all — a 1992 Children's Defense Fund study put 40% of children without employer-provided insurance.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers generally. The bill replaced the income tax rate structure (15%/28%/31%) with 16% on income up to roughly $21,600–$36,000 depending on filing status, 30% above that, and 33% at the top — raising the tax rate on most income, including ordinary workers' wages — and raised the corporate rate from 34% to 37%. Families already covered through work would see the government take over coverage of young children and pregnancy, with employer plans stepping back.

drawbacks.text: The financing raised income tax rates on nearly all taxable income — the base rate rose from 15% to 16%, and the 28% bracket became 30% — so working households that already had coverage would pay more in taxes to fund the new program.

The bill promised that physicians, hospitals, and specialties would not suffer any net loss of income from the program and set payment rates 'fully adequate to compensate providers reasonably,' which limits any savings from moving to a single public payer and would push costs onto taxpayers.

It created a new federal administration to set payment rates and run enrollment, a significant expansion of federal bureaucracy, and coverage of young children would displace existing employer and private insurance in that market.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real and two-sided: a guaranteed, no-cost-sharing health program for every pregnant woman and child under 7 in exchange for higher tax rates on most income and on corporations. The case for it rested on the scale of the gap — 40% of children without employer coverage, half of Medicaid-eligible children unserved, high infant mortality — and the argument that prenatal and preventive care costs less than neonatal intensive care for low-birth-weight babies. The honest objections are that the tax increase reached ordinary households that already had coverage, and that the bill's explicit guarantee against any provider income loss sharply limited the savings a public program could capture. It was a broad, expensive entitlement with provider protections built in — a defensible design choice, but one that raised its cost to taxpayers.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees on the day it was introduced, sent to a Health subcommittee three weeks later, and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before the 102nd Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. James R. Olin introduced the bill on February 18, 1992, and it was referred jointly to the House Committees on Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means.
On March 13, 1992, it was referred to the Energy and Commerce Subcommittee on Health and the Environment; the record shows no further action.
Neither committee reported the bill, no roll-call vote was ever held, and the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993, killing the bill.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers kept the market for covering young children and pregnancy, employers kept responsibility for dependent coverage, and taxpayers avoided the rate increase. Families without coverage for young children and pregnancy gained nothing; the 1992 status quo of uninsured and underinsured children continued into the next Congress.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Insurers and employers; uninsured families gained nothing

for.name: Rep. James R. Olin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and wrote the coverage and financing design, including a finding that 40% of American children lacked employer-provided health insurance.

for.name: 2 House Democratic cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no other House members signed on.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee (Chair John Dingell)
against.role: One of two committees to which the bill was referred
against.what_they_did: Sent the bill to its Health and the Environment subcommittee on March 13, 1992, and never reported it; no markup or vote was held.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee (Chair Dan Rostenkowski)
against.role: Second committee to which the bill was jointly referred, with jurisdiction over the tax provisions
against.what_they_did: Never reported the bill; the financing title raising income and corporate tax rates received no committee action.

sides.party_line_note: No roll-call votes were ever taken; the only members on record were the sponsor and two cosponsors, all Democrats.

industries.note: A universal government plan for all pregnant women and children under 7 would have moved that population out of private coverage, shrinking insurers' market, though the bill let HMOs compete for Medicare-style risk contracts under the new program. Insurers' interest in keeping the commercial market ran against the public alternative the bill offered.

The bill made them the paid providers of a permanent public program and required payment rates 'fully adequate,' with an explicit guarantee that no physician group, specialty, or region would suffer a net income loss. They gained a guaranteed revenue stream but lost the ability to bill patients above the government rate.
The bill allowed contracts with HMOs and competitive medical plans modeled on Medicare's risk-sharing arrangements, giving managed care a formal role inside the new program.
The corporate tax rate would have risen from 34% to 37%, but employers who now pay for pregnancy and young-child coverage would have shed that benefit cost to the public program.
